extra.message: Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads on Request Body — Remote code execution; full server compromise [verified: Duplicate of idx 1 — acct_bundle_thaw_174 passes attacker-controlled bytes to pickle.loads behind only _wrk_gate; confirmed RCE via insecure deserialization.]

Server-Side Template Injection via Jinja2 Template from User Input — Remote code execution; full server and database compromise. [verified: acct_jinja_cast_488 concatenates the user-supplied fragment GET parameter directly into a Jinja2 Template string and calls render(); gated only by _wrk_gate, an attacker with the ops token can supply template expressions for full RCE via SSTI.]

OS Command Injection via Unsanitised host Parameter in os.system — Arbitrary OS command execution as the Django process user; full server compromise. [verified: acct_shell_probe_506 appends the unsanitised host GET parameter to 'ping -c 1 ' and passes it to os.system(); gated only by _wrk_gate, shell metacharacters in host yield arbitrary OS command execution.]

Hardcoded Default Django SECRET_KEY — Forged session cookies granting arbitrary account access; forged CSRF tokens; forged password-reset tokens enabling account takeover for any user. [verified: settings.py line 6 sets SECRET_KEY = os.getenv('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY', 'dev-only-change-me'), and there is no other settings file or environment enforcement that overrides this default. An attacker who knows the default key 'dev-only-change-me' can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, and password-reset tokens for any user.]

Hardcoded Default Django SECRET_KEY — Attacker can forge session cookies and CSRF tokens, leading to session hijacking and authentication bypass [verified: Duplicate of finding [0]: settings.py uses os.getenv('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY', 'dev-only-change-me') and no other mechanism forces a production value; the hardcoded default is publicly known and allows forging of session cookies, CSRF tokens, and password-reset tokens.]

Plaintext PII (SSN/Card) Written to Disk — SSNs and payment card numbers stored in cleartext on the server filesystem; exposed to anyone with filesystem access or directory traversal [verified: Duplicate of idx 14 — acct_vault_stash_239 writes SSN and card in plaintext JSON to disk; confirmed sensitive data exposure.]

Path Traversal and Plaintext PII (SSN/Card) Written to Disk — Arbitrary file write containing attacker-supplied SSN and payment card values anywhere the process can write; also unconditional plaintext storage of SSN/card data. [verified: acct_vault_stash_239 constructs the write path as BASE_EXPORT_DIR / f'{ref}.json' where ref is unsanitised GET input, enabling path traversal, and also writes user-supplied SSN and card values to that file in plaintext; both sub-issues are real and confirmed in the code.]

Plaintext SSN and Payment Card Number Written to Filesystem — SSN and payment card data stored unencrypted on disk; accessible to any user or process that can read the `private_exports/` directory; violates PCI-DSS and data protection regulations. [verified: acct_vault_stash_239 writes SSN and card number (from GET parameters or hardcoded defaults) to a JSON file on disk in plaintext; this is unconditional plaintext PCI/PII storage on the filesystem, confirmed in the code.]

Reflected Origin CORS with Credentials Allowed — Cross-origin requests from any attacker-controlled domain can read authenticated responses, enabling cross-site data theft [verified: Duplicate of idx 7 — acct_origin_mirror_466 reflects Origin into ACAO with credentials allowed; confirmed CORS misconfiguration.]

Path Traversal / Arbitrary File Write via User-Controlled Filename — Arbitrary file write anywhere on the filesystem the process can reach; can overwrite cron jobs, Django settings, or SSH authorized_keys to achieve RCE. [verified: acct_dock_shelf_494 constructs the write path as BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name where name comes directly from GET without sanitisation; path traversal sequences like ../../etc/cron.d/backdoor resolve above the export directory and write arbitrary bytes from request.body, gated only by _wrk_gate.]

Unauthenticated Direct Access to Uploaded Media Files — Any uploaded document (contracts, security questionnaires, invoices) can be downloaded by an unauthenticated attacker who knows or guesses the file URL [verified: Identical root cause to finding [1]: static(settings.MEDIA_URL, document_root=settings.MEDIA_ROOT) serves all uploaded files unauthenticated with no intervening access control, and DEBUG defaults to True (DJANGO_DEBUG env var defaults to '1'), meaning this route is always active in the default configuration.]

Unauthenticated Direct Access to Uploaded Media Files Bypasses Authorization — Any unauthenticated or unauthorized user who knows or can enumerate the media file URL can download any uploaded document — including internal contracts, security questionnaires, and billing-only files — completely bypassing the can_download_document() authorization check. [verified: The media files are served via Django's static() helper which, per the investigation, is active when DEBUG=True (the default) and has no authentication check whatsoever; the document_download view's can_download_document() check is completely bypassed when files are accessed directly via the MEDIA_URL path (e.g., media/organizations/1/documents/contract.pdf). No middleware, reverse proxy, or authe]

Disabled Account Bypass — ensure_enabled Not Called on login_required-Only Views — A user whose account has been disabled (profile.disabled=True) retains full access to their role's login-required endpoints via an existing session; account suspension is ineffective. [verified: No middleware or global mechanism enforces the disabled check; `ensure_enabled` is only called inside `role_required` and `can_access_org`. Views decorated solely with `@login_required` (dashboard, profile, organization_list, escalation_queue, reports, export_csv, etc.) perform no disabled check whatsoever, so a disabled user with a valid session retains full access to those routes.]

Disabled Account Bypass on Management Operations — Disabled users can still perform management operations (create contacts, deals, upload documents, manage API keys) on organizations they previously owned [verified: `can_manage_org` (authz.py line 46) calls only `user_role()` and performs no `ensure_enabled` check, unlike `can_access_org` which calls it on line 28. All write-path views (organization_edit, contact_create, deal_create/edit/delete, document_upload, api_key_create/rotate/revoke, webhook_create/test) route through `can_manage_org`, so a disabled ACCOUNT_MANAGER retains full write access to organiz]

Hardcoded Default Password for Invited Customer Contacts — Any attacker who knows the invited user's email (username) can authenticate with the known password 'DemoPass123!' [verified: Identical core issue as [0] and [2]: the contact_invite function hardcodes 'DemoPass123!' as every invited customer contact's password and discloses it in the UI flash message. This is a real, reachable production flow allowing immediate account compromise for any invited contact.]

Hardcoded Default Password for All Invited Customer Contacts — Any invited customer contact account can be immediately compromised using the publicly known password 'DemoPass123!', enabling unauthorized access to org data, documents, and escalations scoped to that customer. [verified: Same as finding [0]: contact_invite unconditionally sets the hardcoded password 'DemoPass123!' for all newly invited customer contacts and discloses it in a flash message on line 169. This is a real production flow, not a seed-only path, allowing any attacker who knows the invited contact's email to immediately authenticate.]

Authorization Header / Secret Token Written to Logs — Credentials and API tokens exposed in log files, accessible to anyone with log access [verified: Duplicate of idx 8 — account_casefeed_roll_032 logs the Authorization header at WARNING level; confirmed credential exposure in logs.]

Open Redirect via lane Parameter — Phishing attacks; session token theft if combined with other vulnerabilities [verified: Duplicate of idx 6 — account_wayback_card_033 redirects to unvalidated lane parameter; confirmed open redirect.]

Missing Authentication on Public ops Endpoint — Any unauthenticated attacker can call the endpoint; the handle/channel parameters are reflected in the response, enabling user enumeration or probing of the identity subsystem without any credentials. [verified: acct_identity_ping_337 at line 87 has NO call to _wrk_gate and no other authentication check; it is registered publicly at /ops/identity/acct-ping-337/ and reflects handle/channel back in the JSON response to any anonymous caller. This is a confirmed missing-authentication finding.]

Mass Assignment via Unfiltered Payload Update — Attacker can elevate role to 'admin', set approved=true, or manipulate balance/tier in the returned response [verified: Duplicate of idx 15 — acct_workset_rebind_197 calls workset.update(payload) with unfiltered attacker-controlled JSON; confirmed mass assignment.]

Missing Authentication on Public Identity Ping Endpoint — Unauthenticated access to an internal ops endpoint; can also be used to probe system reachability and leak reflected input [verified: This is the same finding as idx 0 — acct_identity_ping_337 has no _wrk_gate call and is publicly accessible; confirmed true positive (duplicate finding, same evidence).]

Hardcoded Credentials / PINs in Source Code — Anyone with source code access can authenticate as any handle; the gate provides no real security [verified: Duplicate of idx 12 — hardcoded PIN map in acct_identity_hint_456 source code; confirmed hardcoded credentials.]

Weak PRNG Used for Security Nonce Generation — Generated nonces/codes are predictable; attacker can brute-force or predict tokens [verified: Duplicate of idx 10 — acct_nonce_roll_516 uses random.choice (non-CSPRNG) for code generation; confirmed weak PRNG for security-sensitive nonces.]

TLS Certificate Verification Disabled for Outbound Requests — MITM attacker can intercept and modify HTTPS responses from the partner endpoint [verified: Duplicate of idx 11 — acct_trust_drift_546 uses ssl._create_unverified_context(); confirmed TLS verification disabled.]

No Rate Limiting on Login and Password-Reset Endpoints — Brute-force attacks against user passwords; mass password-reset email flooding (DoS against email service); account enumeration amplification. [verified: The login view at /accounts/login/ and password-reset at /accounts/password-reset/ use stock Django auth views with no rate-limiting middleware, django-axes, django-ratelimit, or any throttle class configured anywhere in settings.py, urls.py, or middleware; a search of the entire codebase found zero rate-limiting controls. This allows unlimited brute-force and enumeration attempts.]

Missing Secure Cookie Flags (SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE / CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE) — Session and CSRF cookies transmitted over HTTP are susceptible to interception and theft, enabling session hijacking and CSRF bypass against users on non-TLS connections or mixed-content scenarios. [verified: Neither SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE, CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE, SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT, nor SECURE_HSTS_SECONDS appear anywhere in settings.py or any other settings file; Django defaults all of these to False/disabled. Session and CSRF cookies will be sent over plain HTTP without the Secure flag, enabling interception on non-TLS connections.]

DEBUG=True by Default Exposes Full Tracebacks and Configuration — Any unhandled exception (e.g., malformed request) exposes stack traces, SQL queries, environment variables, and partial settings to anonymous attackers. [verified: settings.py line 7 sets DEBUG = os.getenv('DJANGO_DEBUG', '1') == '1', defaulting to True with no override elsewhere; no other settings file overrides this. When DEBUG=True, Django returns full tracebacks with local variables, SQL queries, and settings content to any client on unhandled exceptions, exposing internal configuration to unauthenticated attackers.]

Unrestricted File Upload — No Extension or Content-Type Validation — Upload of server-side executable files (e.g. .py scripts); if the web server is misconfigured, direct execution. Uploaded HTML/SVG files served from the same origin enable stored XSS. [verified: DocumentForm.clean_file only validates file size (5 MB), with no extension allowlist or MIME/magic-byte check, so any file type (.html, .svg, .py, .sh) can be uploaded. However, Django's static() media serving is a no-op when DEBUG=False (the production norm), limiting direct XSS/execution risk to DEBUG=True deployments; the missing content-type validation itself is a real gap but execution on the]

User-Controlled Filename in Document Upload Path — Attacker with can_manage_org permission can upload a file whose name produces a predictable, publicly accessible URL. Combined with the unauthenticated MEDIA_URL serving, this enables stored content injection (HTML/JS files served from the application domain) and potentially path traversal outside the media directory. [verified: document_upload_path does not call os.path.basename() on the filename, so a crafted filename such as '../../2/documents/evil.html' normalises to 'organizations/2/documents/evil.html' (still within MEDIA_ROOT), bypassing validate_file_name and writing into another tenant's document directory — a confirmed cross-tenant file-write path traversal within MEDIA_ROOT.]

CSV Formula Injection in Exported Reports — Malicious formula in a CSV export executes when opened by a staff member in a spreadsheet application, potentially exfiltrating data or executing commands [verified: Same as finding [3]: export_csv writes unsanitized user-controlled strings directly as CSV cells, enabling formula injection (CWE-1236). Real exploitation requires a staff member to open the file in a spreadsheet application and approve formula execution, making this low-severity.]

Unbounded CSV Import File Size — Potential Memory Exhaustion DoS — Server memory exhaustion; denial of service for all users of the application. [verified: The import_data view reads the full uploaded file into memory via uploaded.read() with no explicit size guard; Django's default DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE (2.5 MB) provides some mitigation by raising RequestDataTooBig for in-memory fields, but files spooled to disk above FILE_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE can still be fully read, reducing the practical severity. Access is gated to PLATFORM_ADMIN and ACC]

CSV Formula Injection in Export Endpoints — Attacker who can set an org name, deal name, or escalation title to a formula string (=, +, -, @) causes arbitrary formula execution in spreadsheet applications when staff export and open the CSV, enabling data exfiltration or local command execution. [verified: The export_csv view writes user-controlled fields (org name, deal name, escalation title, assigned agent username) directly into CSV cells via csv.writer with no formula-prefix sanitization, enabling CWE-1236 CSV injection. Exploitation requires a victim (staff member) to open the exported CSV in Excel or LibreOffice and confirm a formula execution warning, significantly limiting real-world impact]

Unbounded CSV Import File — Memory Exhaustion DoS — An ACCOUNT_MANAGER can upload a multi-gigabyte CSV file to /imports/, causing the server to attempt to decode and buffer the entire file in memory, leading to OOM crash or severe performance degradation. [verified: Identical to finding [1]: import_data reads the entire uploaded CSV into memory with no size check, gated only by Django's default 2.5 MB DATA_UPLOAD_MAX_MEMORY_SIZE heuristic which can be bypassed for disk-spooled files. Access requires ACCOUNT_MANAGER or PLATFORM_ADMIN role, limiting the attack surface.]
